title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted Array II
description: Allow each value at most twice in-place using a slow/fast write-pointer pattern.

data.text: Given a sorted array `nums`, remove duplicates **in place** so that each value appears at most twice. Return the new length `k`, and the first `k` elements of `nums` must hold the result. Do not allocate a second array.
Walk the array counting how many times each value appears, then write each value back `min(count, 2)` times. Correct but easy to get wrong with the write index bookkeeping.

data.title: Run counting O(n)
data.content: Count each run, then rewrite it capped at two.

data.text: Use `fast` to read every element and `slow` as the write position. An element is allowed if the last two elements already written are not both equal to it. Because the array is sorted, all equal values are adjacent, so this check is sufficient.

data.title: Write Pointer O(n) time, O(1) space
data.content: One pass, one comparison against the element two positions back.

data.title: Generalise to "at most k" by changing one number
data.text: The condition `slow < 2 || value != nums[slow - 2]` becomes `slow < k || value != nums[slow - k]` for 'each value at most k times'. This is the classic version of this problem.

data.title: Do not compare against the input position
data.text: Compare the incoming value with `nums[slow - 2]`, the already-written output, not `nums[fast - 2]`, which may have been overwritten earlier in this same pass.

data.caption: fast reads every value; slow only advances when the value is not a third copy of the run.
data.definition:
graph LR
    A["[1,1,1,2,2,3]"] --> B["write 1 (slow=1)"]
    B --> C["write 1 (slow=2)"]
    C --> D["third 1: nums[0]=1 == 1 -> skip"]
    D --> E["write 2 (slow=3)"]
    E --> F["write 2 (slow=4)"]
    F --> G["third 2? no: 3 != 2 -> write 3 (slow=5)"]
    G --> H["return 5"]
    style H fill:#e8f5e9,stroke:#2e7d32

cards.title: Write pointer
cons: The `slow < 2` guard looks like a special case

data.title: Complete solution
data.content: The pattern of reading with a fast index and writing with a slow index is how every in-place array compaction problem is solved — removing elements, moving zeroes, merging sorted arrays, and this one.
